statement: In people who smoked and were motivated to quit, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials comparing ways of using nicotine replacement (Cochrane review, search to April 2022; 16 trials with 12,169 people for combination use, 8 trials with 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch), combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form such as gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray), compared with a single form, increased the number not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt: about 4 more people in 100 (174 against 137 in 1,000, 95% CI 160 to 187; risk ratio 1.27, 1.17 to 1.37; I² 12%; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). The ratio was similar against the patch alone (1.24, 1.13 to 1.37; 13 trials) and against a fast-acting form alone (1.30, 1.09 to 1.54; 6 trials); a third subgroup, one trial in which most people were lost to follow-up, gave a much larger ratio (5.16, 1.18 to 22.59). It was unchanged without the trials at high risk of bias, and a funnel plot of the 16 trials showed no sign of publication bias, which the authors read with caution because the number is small. A fast-acting form alone (lozenge, nasal spray, gum or inhaler), compared with the patch, showed no clear difference: 148 against 164 in 1,000, about 2 fewer in 100 with fast-acting forms (interval 4 fewer to 1 more; risk ratio 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05; I² 0%; 8 trials, one of them in adolescents; unchanged without the high-risk trials or the adolescent trial), with no clear difference for any single form (lozenge 0.94, 3 trials; nasal spray 0.90, 2 trials; gum 0.58, 2 trials and 118 people; inhaler 0.59, 1 trial and 222 people), so the interval does not rule out the patch doing somewhat better. People in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day on average, so the results say little about lighter smoking; the review's comparisons of doses, lengths of use and timing, which gave mixed results, are not covered here. By the editors' count 9 of the 16 combination trials and 6 of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials named a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors; the review judged company funding less relevant to comparisons between ways of using nicotine replacement and did not assess it. Certainty: high. Status: replicated.
plain: When trials compared ways of using nicotine replacement, people who used a patch plus a fast-acting form, such as gum or lozenges, did better than people who used one form alone: about 17 in 100 were not smoking 6 months or more later, against about 14 in 100, so about 4 more in 100. A fast-acting form on its own and the patch showed no clear difference, though the trials cannot rule out the patch doing a little better (about 2 fewer in 100 with fast-acting forms; the range runs from 4 fewer to 1 more). Many of the trials were backed by the makers of the products, and the review did not check whether that changed the results.
population: People who smoked and were motivated to quit, mostly smoking about 20 or more cigarettes a day, in randomised and quasi-randomised trials of ways of using nicotine replacement (68 trials, 43,327 people in the review; 16 trials, 12,169 people for combination use; 8 trials, 3,319 people for fast-acting forms against the patch); Cochrane review, search to April 2022
exposure: Combination nicotine replacement (a patch plus a fast-acting form: gum, lozenge, inhaler or nasal spray); a fast-acting form alone
comparator: A single form of nicotine replacement (patch alone, or a fast-acting form alone); for the fast-acting forms, the nicotine patch
outcome: Not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt (strictest definition, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
magnitude: Combination vs single form: RR 1.27 (95% CI 1.17–1.37), I² 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; 137 vs 174 per 1,000 (160–187), about 4 more in 100 (editors' subtraction: 37 per 1,000). Against patch alone 1.24 (1.13–1.37; 13 studies; 9,552; I² 28%); against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09–1.54; 6; 2,364; I² 0%); against a choice of single form 5.16 (1.18–22.59; 1 study; 253; high risk of bias). Fast-acting form vs patch: RR 0.90 (0.77–1.05), I² 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 vs 148 per 1,000 (126–172), about 2 fewer in 100 (interval 4 fewer to 1 more, editors' subtraction). By form: lozenge 0.94 (0.79–1.12; 3; 1,707), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64–1.27; 2; 1,272), gum 0.58 (0.26–1.31; 2; 118), inhaler 0.59 (0.22–1.60; 1; 222).

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1; Analysis 4.1
evidence.extracted: Combination NRT (patch plus a fast-acting form) against single-form NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 1.27 (1.17 to 1.37), I² 12%, 16 studies, 12,169 participants; 137 per 1,000 with a single form against 174 per 1,000 (160 to 187) with combination (editors' subtraction: about 4 in 100). The authors rate it high certainty; the estimate was unchanged without the high-risk trials.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 1st paragraph; Analysis 4.1.1 to 4.1.3; Characteristics of included studies › Dignan 2019
evidence.extracted: Subgroups: against patch alone RR 1.24 (1.13 to 1.37), I² 28%, 13 studies, 9,552 participants (the text prints 9,522; the table's subgroups sum to the pool's 12,169); against a fast-acting form alone 1.30 (1.09 to 1.54), I² 0%, 6 studies, 2,364; against a choice of a single form 5.16 (1.18 to 22.59), 1 study, 253 (Dignan 2019, high risk of bias because most participants were lost to follow-up). No clear subgroup difference (I² 45.8%, P = 0.16).

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Combination therapy › Combination versus single form, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 (as described in the text); Discussion › Potential biases in the review process
evidence.extracted: The funnel plot for the 16 combination studies, the only comparison with 10 or more studies, gave no evidence of publication bias, which the authors say should be read with caution because the number of studies is small.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Fast-acting NRT versus patch, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 5; Analysis 6.1
evidence.extracted: Fast-acting NRT against the nicotine patch, abstinence at 6 months or longer: RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.05), I² 0%, 8 studies, 3,319 participants; 164 per 1,000 with the patch against 148 per 1,000 (126 to 172) with a fast-acting form (editors' subtraction: about 2 fewer in 100, interval 4 fewer to 1 more). By form: inhaler 0.59 (0.22 to 1.60; 1 study; 222), nasal spray 0.90 (0.64 to 1.27; 2; 1,272), lozenge 0.94 (0.79 to 1.12; 3; 1,707), gum 0.58 (0.26 to 1.31; 2; 118). The authors rate it high certainty; no subgroup difference (P = 0.57). The overall effect was not sensitive to removing high-risk studies or, post hoc, Moolchan 2005, a trial in adolescents.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Potential biases in the review process; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice
evidence.extracted: The authors limit generalisation to adults motivated to quit who smoke about 20 or more cigarettes a day (highest mean 38) and say there is little evidence for people smoking fewer than 15 a day; e-cigarettes are not covered; unpublished data may be missing; reference lists were not screened uniformly across versions.

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Tables 1 and 5 footnotes
evidence.extracted: Of 68 trials, 9 low risk of bias in every domain, 28 high in at least one, 31 unclear. Removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for preloading (outside this claim); the footnotes to the combination and fast-acting-against-patch rows say that restricting to low-risk studies gave a consistent estimate and confidence interval.

evidence.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count); Discussion › Certainty of the evidence, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Editors' count of the 68 trials: 38 name a manufacturer as funder, sponsor, supplier of product or employer of authors (20 as funder or sponsor); 23 name none; 7 report no source. Of the 16 combination trials 9 involve a manufacturer (4 funded or sponsored by Pharmacia or employing its staff, 5 through product supply or affiliation) and 7 do not; of the 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials 6 do, 1 names none and 1 reports no source. The review states that it did not assess bias from industry funding, judging it less applicable to comparisons between ways of using NRT.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Patch therapy › Dose and Duration; Fast-acting NRT › Gum dose; NRT preloading versus standard post-quit use; Summary of findings, Tables 2, 3, 4 and 7
evidence.extracted: Comparisons outside this claim, held on the study card: a higher against a lower patch dose favoured the higher dose in two of three comparisons (moderate certainty; in one of the two the lower confidence limit was 1.00); 4 mg against 2 mg gum favoured the higher strength overall but only in a post hoc higher-dependence subgroup; starting before the quit date favoured early use (RR 1.25) but not once high-risk trials were removed (1.16); no clear difference for patch duration, combination duration, tapering, fixed against as-needed use, gum duration or free against purchased NRT, mostly from one or two small trials.

publication_bias.note: Funnel plot for 16 combination trials symmetric (authors urge caution); manufacturer links in 9 of 16 combination trials and 6 of 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials, not assessed by the review.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane review (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card) whose two pools used here the review rates high. Risk of bias, not rated down: 9 of 68 trials were low risk in every domain and 28 high in at least one, but the review reports that restricting each pool to low-risk trials gave a consistent estimate and that removing high-risk trials changed the interpretation only for the timing comparison, which is outside this claim. Inconsistency, not rated down (I² 12% for combination use, 0% for fast-acting forms against the patch). Indirectness, not rated down: the claim is limited to people motivated to quit who smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day in trials. Imprecision, not rated down: the combination interval (1.17 to 1.37) is far from no difference; the fast-acting-against-patch result is reported as no clear difference with its whole interval (0.77 to 1.05), which does not exclude a quit rate about a fifth lower with fast-acting forms, and the claim says so; the review's high rating rests on 3,319 people. Publication bias, not rated down: the funnel plot for combination use (16 trials) shows no asymmetry, though the authors caution that 16 is few, and the fast-acting-against-patch pool has too few trials for a funnel plot. The editors record that a manufacturer is linked to 9 of 16 combination trials and 6 of 8 fast-acting-against-patch trials (editors' count), that the review did not assess this, and that a stricter reading, taking company-linked trials as a possible source of inflation, would give moderate. Status replicated: the combination result is pooled from 16 trials by many groups with little heterogeneity. The 2018 review of nicotine replacement against control and this review may share trials (not checked); this claim rests on this review alone.

verification.flag_note: Staged separately from cl_nic_nrt (against placebo or no replacement) so that the head-to-head result keeps its own rating; the senior author may merge them. Certainty follows Cochrane's high rating for both comparisons. Deliberately left out of the claim (on the Theodoulou study card only): patch dose and duration, gum strength, combination duration, tapering, fixed against as-needed use, timing before the quit date, free against purchased replacement and who chose the product; they gave mixed results and several rest on one or two small trials. The abstract of the 2023 review calls the 4 mg against 2 mg gum result high certainty without a summary-of-findings table or GRADE rating (see the card); it is not used. Not read: Appendix 3, trial-level risk-of-bias tables, forest and funnel figures (images). Four three-arm trials (Croghan 2003, Tønnesen 2000, Piper 2009, Smith 2009) feed both single-form subgroups; how the shared combination arm was handled was not checked. No new reference is needed (theodoulou_2023 exists).
